newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia says won't target trade in Iran row.
newsitem.headline: Australia says won't target trade in Iran row.

text.p: Australia said on Wednesday it would not hit trade with Iran and would stick to diplomatic sanctions against the Islamic state after a German court linked Tehran to terrorism.

Deputy Prime Minister and Trade Minister Tim Fischer, who has argued trade and politics should remain separate, moved to reassure wheat farmers the government was not considering trade sanctions against their biggest market, worth A$500 million (US390 million) a year.

"Australia does not seek to interfere with the commercial negotiations, be it by the Australian Wheat Board, by a large company or by a small company, with regard to the two-way trade that exists between Australia and Iran," he told reporters.
The Labor opposition had urged an immediate trade ban and the cancellation of a A$950 million line of credit, even though Australia has a large trade surplus with Iran.

Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Tuesday Canberra would consider further action against Iran after consultations with key allies, including the United States and European powers, and a detailed examination of the German court verdict.
But he confirmed the government was reviewing the unused line of credit with Tehran.
The Australian Wheat Board, which oversees wheat sales, said earlier on Wednesday it was confident trade with Iran would not be hit.
"Both sides would be reluctant to put trade in jeopardy," board chairman Trevor Flugge said.
Australia is exporting up to three million tonnes of wheat to Iran in the fiscal year to June 30, 1997, worth about A$500 million.
"It is a matter that Australia does not seek to interfere with commercial activities between companies large and small ... as things stand between Australia and Iran," Fischer said.
Two-way trade is heavily in Australia's favour -- A$650 million in Australian exports and A$28 million in imports from Iran in calendar 1996, including wheat.
A German court last week ruled Iran's political leadership had ordered the killings of a group of Iranian Kurdish leaders in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant in 1992.

It avoided names but said the assassination was ordered by a secret special operations committee whose members included Iran's president, religious leader, intelligence minister and head of foreign policy. Tehran denies supporting terrorism.
